items.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003
items.q: And had a lot of great people who came through there teaching and sharing there, from Don Friedman and Frank Foster to

ctx.x: I know you retired very recently from —

1999, I was retired after 28 years at Rutgers. I build the undergraduate degree program there, and the master’s program there in jazz. I helped shepherd that. And I was very fortunate in that I was the first and only, at that time, and I don’t know if it’s changing now but I had four tenured professors in jazz. And four of them African-American. The first person I brought in was Ted Dunbar. Second person Kenny Baron. Then Bill Fielder and then of course myself. And had a lot of great people who came through there…
been jazz artist in residence at the Schomburg Center which is a part of the New York Public Library.

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: At Davidson College of Rutgers University I was one of the jazz professors under Larry Ridley, with Ted Dunbar, Kenny Barron, and the late Freddie Waits.

ctx.x: Funking in Jamaica I think was his big thing, on Arista.

Yeah, I wanted him to be there more often, but at that time he was just getting ready to get busy, so he couldn’t some around too much. At Davidson College of Rutgers University I was one of the jazz professors under Larry Ridley, with Ted Dunbar, Kenny Barron, and the late Freddie Waits. We had a quintet called the Jazz Professors. We went to Senegal -- not Senegal. Lesotho in southern Africa -- on a two-week educational tour and concert tour in which Dizzy Gillespie participated and the late Monk Montgomery as…
Joe was at Central State when I was at Antioch.
